@@124479689 <h> The Enduring Resonance : Contemporary Relevance of Jesus Christ 's Core Messages in a World of Islamophobia , Hate Campaigns , and Civilizational Conflict <h> Share : <p> Jesus of Nazareth , a figure whose life and teachings , chronicled primarily in the Gospels of the New Testament , fundamentally shaped the trajectory of Western civilization and continue to exert profound influence on billions across the globe , delivered a corpus of messages that resonate with startling potency in the complex landscape of the 21st century . Though originating two millennia ago within the unique socio-political milieu of Roman-occupied Judea , these teachings , when examined beyond specific theological interpretations and through an ecumenical lens , offer enduring ethical wisdom . Viewed variously within diverse Christian denominations and by other faiths and secular perspectives , certain core ethical injunctions attributed to Jesus transcend cultural and temporal divides , providing potent resources for navigating contemporary challenges marked by escalating Islamophobia , pervasive hatred campaigns , and the looming spectre of civilizational conflict . This paper aims to explore the contemporary relevance of three interconnected clusters of Jesus 's core messages @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ history to illuminate their persistent power . We will delve into the foundational principle of empathetic love , encompassing the call to love one 's neighbour as oneself and the Golden Rule ; the radical extension of this love to encompass even enemies ; and the crucial inner discipline of humility and non-judgment , symbolized by the parable of the speck and the plank . By thoroughly scanning the evidence and arguments presented across various analyses of these teachings , without omission but avoiding duplication , we can construct a comprehensive understanding of their applicability to fostering individual well-being , interpersonal harmony , and societal progress in our turbulent times . <p> The world today stands at a precarious juncture , characterized by both unprecedented interconnectedness facilitated by technology and deep , often violent , fragmentation along lines of religion , ethnicity , nationality , and ideology . Hatred campaigns , often fuelled by political expediency and amplified by digital media , target vulnerable groups , fostering climates of fear and dehumanization . Islamophobia , a specific and virulent form of prejudice directed towards Muslims and perceived Islamic culture , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and even violence . Broader anxieties about " civilizational conflict , " pitting monolithic cultural blocs against each other , further poison international relations and hinder cooperative solutions to global problems like climate change , pandemics , and economic inequality . It is precisely within this context of division , animosity , and judgment that the ethical core of Jesus 's teachings demands renewed attention , offering not simplistic solutions , but a profound reorientation of human relationships based on empathy , forgiveness , and humility . <p> The Foundation : Empathy , Reciprocity , and the Love of Neighbour <p> Perhaps the most universally recognized distillation of Jesus Christ 's ethical framework resides in the commandment identified as the second greatest , intricately linked to the primary commandment of loving God : " Love your neighbour as yourself . " This injunction appears consistently across the Synoptic Gospels ( Mark 12:31 , Matthew 22:39 , Luke 10:27 ) and builds upon , yet significantly expands , the foundation laid in the Hebrew Bible ( Leviticus 19:18 ) . In its original Levitical context , " neighbour " primarily @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ your brother , " " the sons of your own people . " Jesus , however , radically redefined and universalized this concept . This ethical cornerstone is intrinsically tied to the principle widely known as the Golden Rule : " So whatever you wish that others would do to you , do also to them , for this is the Law and the Prophets " ( Matthew 7:12 ) , with a similar formulation in Luke 6:31 . Together , these twin principles constitute the bedrock of a relational ethic grounded fundamentally in empathy -- the capacity to understand and share the feelings of another -- and reciprocity -- the practice of exchanging things with others for mutual benefit . <p> The contemporary relevance of this dual principle is immense , perhaps more so than ever , in a world simultaneously hyper-connected through digital technology and global travel , yet paradoxically plagued by profound fragmentation , alienation , and tribalism . The very definition of " neighbour " becomes a crucial point of contention . Jesus directly addressed this through the powerful Parable of the Good Samaritan ( Luke @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ law about the identity of his neighbour , Jesus narrated a story where established religious figures ignored a suffering man , while a Samaritan -- a member of a group despised by and hostile towards Jews -- demonstrated compassionate care . The parable culminates not with a definition , but with a question that reverses the perspective : " Which of these three do you think was a neighbour to the man who fell into the hands of robbers ? " The answer identifies the one who showed mercy . Thus , Jesus subverts definitions based on geography , ethnicity , religion , or social standing . The neighbour is not simply someone like us or near us , but anyone we encounter who is in need , challenging the listener to become a neighbour through compassionate action . <p> This radical expansion directly confronts modern tendencies towards nationalism , ethnocentrism , xenophobia , and indifference to distant suffering . In an era marked by unprecedented global migration , escalating refugee crises driven by conflict and climate change , and vast , persistent economic inequality , the call to love @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , the marginalized , the perceived " other , " the person holding different beliefs or belonging to a different culture -- as oneself demands a fundamental expansion of our circle of moral concern . It directly challenges ideologies and practices like racism , caste systems , social stratification , and specifically , Islamophobia , which seeks to define Muslims as inherently alien , threatening , and undeserving of the empathy and respect we reserve for our " own . " Jesus 's teaching urges the recognition of a shared , fundamental humanity that transcends these socially constructed divisions , demanding we treat others with the dignity and care we intrinsically desire for ourselves . <p> The power of this ethical injunction finds compelling resonance with insights from modern science . Neuroscience , for instance , has identified the existence of " mirror neurons " -- brain cells that fire both when an individual performs an action and when they observe the same action performed by another ( Iacoboni , 2009 ) . This neurological mechanism is widely considered a biological underpinning for empathy , suggesting that our brains are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ vicariously experience the states of others . Research in positive psychology and public health consistently demonstrates the tangible benefits of cultivating such empathetic connection and engaging in prosocial behaviour . Altruism , acts of kindness , and strong social connections are significantly correlated with increased individual happiness , improved mental health , greater life satisfaction , enhanced resilience to stress , and even increased longevity ( Post , 2005 ; Davidson &amp; McEwen , 2012 ) . Conversely , social isolation , perceived discrimination , and chronic loneliness are identified as major risk factors for a range of poor physical and mental health outcomes . Loving one 's neighbour , therefore , is not merely a moral ideal but aligns with pathways to human flourishing recognized by science . <p> From a sociological perspective , the principles of loving the neighbour and the Golden Rule are fundamental to building and sustaining healthy communities . Concepts like " social capital , " popularized by Robert Putnam ( 2000 ) , refer to the networks , norms of reciprocity , and social trust that facilitate coordination and cooperation for mutual benefit . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to the Golden Rule and extending care to one 's neighbours . Societies characterized by higher levels of social capital tend to exhibit more effective governance , stronger economic performance , better public health outcomes , lower crime rates , and greater overall resilience in the face of crises , as seen in communities with robust mutual aid networks . The COVID-19 pandemic , for example , underscored the practical necessity of collective well-being and neighbourly love , as societies prioritizing mutual care and public health measures often fared better than those emphasizing radical individualism . <p> Historically , the ethical core expressed in the Golden Rule demonstrates remarkable universality . Variations of this principle -- both positive ( " Do unto others ... " ) and negative ( " Do not do unto others ... " ) -- appear across numerous cultures , religions , and philosophical traditions , including Confucianism ( shu ) , Hinduism ( dharma ) , Islam ( Quran and Hadith ) , Judaism ( as cited by Jesus ) , Buddhism ( Metta Sutta ) , and ancient Greek philosophy ( Wattles , 1996 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fundamental , perhaps even essential , principle for maintaining stable social order and facilitating human interaction . Its underlying logic forms the implicit ethical basis for modern international human rights declarations , which assert the inherent dignity and equal worth of all individuals , demanding a standard of treatment that we would reasonably expect and desire for ourselves . Historically , this principle has fuelled movements for social justice and reform , from the early Christian communities known for their care of the poor ( Acts 4:32-35 ) to the abolitionist movement led by figures like William Wilberforce , who saw slavery as a violation of neighbourly love , to modern humanitarian organizations like Habitat for Humanity , Doctors Without Borders , and the International Red Cross , which operationalize this teaching on a global scale , transcending national and religious boundaries . <p> In the specific context of the digital age , the call to love neighbours as self and abide by the Golden Rule acquires critical urgency . Online environments , often characterized by anonymity or pseudonymity , can unfortunately foster disinhibition , leading to cyberbullying , harassment @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and the formation of echo chambers that amplify division and hostility . Screens can facilitate a dangerous dehumanization , making it easier to treat others as abstractions or targets rather than fellow human beings deserving of respect . Applying the Golden Rule in digital interactions demands mindful communication , resisting impulsive attacks , verifying information before sharing , engaging with differing viewpoints respectfully ( even in disagreement ) , and consciously striving to foster online communities built on mutual regard rather than antagonism . Campaigns promoting empathy and kindness online ( e.g. , #BeKind ) implicitly draw upon this fundamental ethic . <p> Ecumenically , the commandment to love one 's neighbour and the principle of the Golden Rule are universally embraced across Christian denominations as foundational ethical imperatives . They provide essential common ground for inter-Christian dialogue , cooperation on social justice initiatives , and engagement in broader interfaith contexts . The Charter for Compassion , endorsed by leaders across various religions , explicitly applies this teaching to global ethics , advocating for policies prioritizing universal human welfare . Furthermore , the teaching invites reflection on the " as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ one 's own inherent dignity and worth , distinct from narcissism -- is intertwined with the ability to love others . Psychological research on self-compassion ( Neff , 2011 ) supports this , showing that individuals who treat themselves with kindness are less prone to depression and anxiety and often exhibit greater compassion towards others . This interconnectedness is particularly relevant in contexts of historical marginalization ( e.g. , postcolonial settings ) where affirming self-worth is a crucial step towards extending solidarity . <p> The Radical Challenge : Loving Enemies and Breaking Cycles of Violence <p> Building upon the already demanding foundation of universal neighbourly love , Jesus introduces an even more radical , counter-intuitive , and profoundly challenging ethical injunction : " Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you " ( Matthew 5:44 ; cf. Luke 6:27-36 ) . This command moves decisively beyond the logic of reciprocity inherent in the Golden Rule ( " Do unto others as you would have them do unto you " ) towards proactive , unconditional goodwill directed specifically towards adversaries , persecutors , and those who inflict harm . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , vengeance , defensiveness , and the primal " fight or flight " response when faced with perceived threats or hostility . In a world saturated with conflict at every level -- from bitter interpersonal disputes and family breakdowns , to acrimonious political polarization within nations , to protracted international wars , ethnic cleansing , and acts of terrorism -- this teaching offers a revolutionary , albeit extraordinarily difficult , alternative pathway . <p> The contemporary relevance of loving one 's enemies lies precisely in its transformative potential to interrupt and ultimately break endemic cycles of violence , hatred , and retribution . Retaliation , however instinctively satisfying or seemingly justified it may feel , almost inevitably breeds further retaliation . An eye for an eye , as Gandhi ( though Hindu , deeply influenced by the Sermon on the Mount ) is often quoted as saying , leaves the whole world blind . Violence begets violence , locking individuals , communities , ethnic groups , and nations into destructive , often escalating patterns of conflict that inflict immense suffering and impede progress . Loving one 's enemy , in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , signifying selfless , willed love focused on the other 's ultimate good , rather than philia or eros ) , does not necessarily imply feeling affection , liking the enemy , agreeing with their actions , or naively ignoring danger . Crucially , as clarified in theological interpretations , it does not mean enabling abuse , endorsing evil , or failing to pursue justice or establish appropriate boundaries for protection . Rather , it entails a fundamental refusal to dehumanize the " other , " even when they are actively hostile . It involves a conscious commitment to seeking their ultimate well-being and potential transformation , even while potentially holding them accountable for their actions through just means . It signifies a persistent willingness to explore avenues for reconciliation , dialogue , and restorative justice rather than succumbing solely to the logic of vengeance and perpetual enmity . <p> This principle speaks with particular force to situations of intractable political conflict , long-standing historical grievances , and deeply entrenched prejudices that fuel contemporary crises . It directly challenges the pervasive rhetoric of demonization used to mobilize populations for war @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ diverse religious group is often painted as a monolithic enemy ) , and underpin ideologies of hate that categorize entire groups as inherently evil or subhuman . By insisting on the humanity even of the adversary , Jesus 's teaching provides a moral anchor against the currents of collective hatred . <p> From a psychological perspective , the concept of loving enemies is closely intertwined with the practice of forgiveness . Extensive research , such as that conducted by Everett Worthington Jr . ( 2005 ) and initiatives like the Stanford Forgiveness Project , demonstrates significant psychological and physiological benefits for the person who forgives . While forgiveness is distinct from reconciliation ( which requires the participation of the other party ) and does not mean condoning the offense , the act of releasing anger , bitterness , resentment , and desires for revenge is strongly linked to reduced levels of stress hormones , lower anxiety and depression rates , improved cardiovascular health , and greater overall emotional well-being . Holding onto hatred and grudges , conversely , is psychologically corrosive and detrimental to health . The capacity to move @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the narrative and cultivating empathy , is psychologically liberating . Loving enemies , therefore , can be understood partly as an act of profound self-care , freeing oneself from the toxic burden of perpetual animosity . Carl Rogers ' emphasis on " unconditional positive regard " in therapeutic contexts also echoes this principle , highlighting the healing potential of acceptance and empathy , even in difficult relationships . <p> Sociologically and politically , the difficult ideal of loving enemies finds partial expression in various approaches to conflict resolution and transitional justice . Restorative justice models , increasingly used in schools , communities , and even some criminal justice systems , prioritize repairing the harm caused by conflict or crime and rebuilding relationships , rather than focusing solely on punitive measures . These processes often involve dialogue between victims , offenders , and community members , aiming for understanding , accountability , and healing . On a larger scale , Truth and Reconciliation Commissions ( TRCs ) , most famously exemplified by South Africa 's post-Apartheid TRC chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu ( 1999 ) , represent attempts to address widespread @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ acknowledgment of suffering , and pathways towards forgiveness and reconciliation , rather than opting for cycles of retribution or blanket amnesty that ignores past wrongs . While the outcomes of such initiatives are often fragile , complex , and incomplete , they offer powerful glimpses of how societies can , against immense odds , attempt to move beyond deeply ingrained cycles of enmity by embracing principles resonant with enemy-love . Interfaith peace initiatives in conflict zones like Northern Ireland , the Middle East , the Balkans , and Kashmir often draw explicitly on religious teachings , including Jesus 's call , to foster dialogue and bridge seemingly insurmountable divides . <p> Historically , the ideal of loving enemies , however challenging , has inspired some of the most potent and transformative movements for nonviolent social and political change . Mahatma Gandhi explicitly cited the Sermon on the Mount as a key influence on his philosophy of satyagraha ( truth force ) and ahimsa ( nonviolence ) , which proved instrumental in India 's struggle for independence . Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. , a Baptist minister , consistently and explicitly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Christian concept of agape love , arguing that nonviolent resistance , even in the face of brutal persecution , was not only strategically effective but morally imperative , aiming to redeem both the oppressed and the oppressor ( King , 1963 ) . Nelson Mandela 's remarkable leadership in guiding South Africa through its transition from apartheid , prioritizing national unity and reconciliation over retribution against former oppressors , stands as a complex but profound political application of this ethic on a national scale . Of course , history is also replete with examples where this ideal was dismissed as utterly naive , impractical , or even dangerous in the face of real threats and aggression . Its implementation remains one of the most profound challenges of the Christian faith and human ethics . <p> Ecumenically , the call to love one 's enemies is universally recognized across Christian traditions as one of the most demanding and distinguishing features of Jesus 's teachings . It is often understood not merely as a human ethical striving but as an imitation of Christ 's own self-sacrificial love demonstrated on the cross @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ central point of theological reflection , ethical struggle , and spiritual discipline for believers , constantly pushing them towards profound personal transformation and challenging participation in systems built on enmity and violence . <p> The Inner Discipline : Humility , Non-Judgment , and Self-Reflection <p> Complementing the outwardly focused commands to love neighbour and enemy is an essential , inwardly focused discipline centered on humility , non-judgment , and rigorous self-reflection . Jesus issues a stern and direct warning : " Do not judge , or you too will be judged . For in the same way you judge others , you will be judged , and with the measure you use , it will be measured to you " ( Matthew 7:1-2 ; cf. Luke 6:37 ) . This principle is then vividly illustrated through the memorable and somewhat humorous metaphor of the speck and the plank : " Why do you look at the speck of sawdust in your brother 's eye and pay no attention to the plank in your own eye ? How can you say to your brother , ' Let me take the speck @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ there is a plank in your own eye ? You hypocrite , first take the plank out of your own eye , and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother 's eye " ( Matthew 7:3-5 ; cf. Luke 6:41-42 ) . Together , these teachings constitute a powerful call for profound self-awareness , intellectual humility , and prioritizing personal moral inventory before engaging in the critique or correction of others . <p> The contemporary relevance of this message is starkly evident in an era often characterized by a pervasive culture of judgment , amplified exponentially by digital media but present across many spheres of life . Social media platforms frequently devolve into arenas for instant condemnation , public shaming ( " cancel culture " ) , performative moral grandstanding , and self-righteous pronouncements , often based on incomplete information or driven by tribal loyalties . Political discourse is increasingly dominated by harsh judgments , the attribution of malicious motives to opponents rather than engaging with their arguments , and Manichean narratives that divide the world into simplistic categories of good and evil , thereby @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ exacerbating societal polarization . Jesus 's teaching directly challenges this pervasive culture of condemnation by insisting on introspection as the necessary first step . <p> It is crucial to understand , as clarified by contextual readings , that this teaching is not an absolute prohibition against all forms of discernment , evaluation , or holding others accountable . Jesus himself engaged in sharp critiques of religious hypocrisy and injustice , and elsewhere advises discernment ( e.g. , John 7:24 : " Stop judging by mere appearances , but instead judge correctly " ) . The target of his warning in Matthew 7 and Luke 6 is specifically hypocritical , condemnatory , and self-righteous judgment -- the kind that eagerly points out the faults of others while conveniently ignoring or excusing one 's own , often more significant , failings . The metaphor of the speck and the plank does not forbid helping one 's brother remove the speck , but it establishes a crucial prerequisite : address your own larger issues first ( " remove the plank " ) to gain the clarity and humility necessary to offer help constructively @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Modern psychological research provides compelling insights into why this teaching is both profoundly necessary and incredibly difficult to practice . Humans are subject to a range of cognitive biases that inherently facilitate judgment of others while simultaneously protecting our own self-image . The " fundamental attribution error , " first described by Lee Ross ( 1977 ) , highlights our pervasive tendency to attribute other people 's negative behaviours primarily to their internal character or disposition , while attributing our own negative behaviours largely to external circumstances or situational factors . " Confirmation bias " leads us to selectively seek out , interpret , and recall information in a way that confirms our pre-existing beliefs and prejudices , reinforcing stereotypes and making us resistant to evidence that challenges our judgments . The " Dunning-Kruger effect , " identified by Kruger and Dunning ( 1999 ) , suggests that individuals with low competence in a particular area often significantly overestimate their own ability , leading to unwarranted confidence in their judgments and opinions . Furthermore , " self-serving bias " makes us attribute successes to our own efforts and failures to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ conviction that we perceive reality objectively and that those who disagree with us must be biased , irrational , or ill-intentioned . Cultivating humility , conversely -- recognizing the limits of our knowledge , acknowledging our fallibility , and being open to correction -- is psychologically associated with better learning outcomes , stronger interpersonal relationships , greater tolerance for ambiguity , and reduced prejudice . Removing the " plank " of our own biases , assumptions , and unacknowledged flaws is therefore essential not only for ethical integrity but also for clearer perception and more compassionate , effective interaction with others . Mindfulness practices , which encourage non-judgmental awareness of one 's own thoughts and feelings , have also been shown to reduce prejudice and improve interpersonal relationships , aligning with Jesus ' call for introspection . <p> Sociologically , the principle of non-judgment and the call for humility directly undermine the foundations of prejudice , stereotyping , and discrimination . These harmful social phenomena rely heavily on making broad , often negative generalizations and judgments about entire groups of people ( based on race , religion , nationality , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ complexity , situational factors , or , crucially , examining our own potential biases and complicity in systemic inequalities . Jesus 's teaching fosters empathy by encouraging us to consider the circumstances , pressures , and internal struggles of others before rushing to condemnation . It resists the tendency , critiqued by sociologists like Zygmunt Bauman ( 2000 ) , to categorize and label people in ways that lead to ethical indifference or dehumanization . Historically , the devastating consequences of unchecked judgmentalism , moral certainty , and hypocrisy are tragically evident in countless episodes of persecution , violence , and atrocity committed in the name of religious purity or ideological righteousness , from religious inquisitions and witch hunts to political purges and genocides . Wisdom traditions across diverse cultures consistently emphasize the importance of self-reflection and self-knowledge as prerequisites for genuine ethical understanding and virtuous action . Paulo Freire 's concept of " conscientization " -- critical self-awareness , particularly regarding one 's role in systems of oppression -- resonates strongly with the call to remove the plank from one 's own eye before critiquing societal structures or others @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ institutions , both religious and secular . The moral integrity of any group or organization depends significantly on its capacity for self-critique , acknowledging failures , and undertaking necessary reforms . History shows numerous instances where religious institutions failed to live up to their own ideals , becoming complicit in injustices like colonialism , slavery , or shielding abusers . Similarly , secular institutions must continually confront issues like structural racism , economic exploitation , and environmental degradation . The call to remove the plank applies collectively as well as individually . It is also crucial for effective leadership ; research indicates that leaders who demonstrate humility , acknowledge their limitations , and are willing to learn from mistakes inspire far greater trust , engagement , and productivity than those who project an image of infallibility and are quick to blame others . <p> Ecumenically , the call to humility and non-judgment resonates profoundly within all Christian traditions . Its wisdom finds echoes and support in contemporary scientific understandings of empathy 's biological roots , psychological research on well-being , sociological observations of thriving communities built on social capital and mutual trust , and its near-universal appearance in diverse ethical traditions across history . <p> The radical and counter-intuitive call to love one 's enemies offers a transformative , albeit profoundly difficult , alternative to the seemingly endless cycles of violence , retribution , and escalating conflict that plague human relations at all levels . They challenge every individual , community , and nation to continually bridge the gap between professed ideals and actual practices , reminding us that the arduous path towards a better shared future requires the intentional cultivation of empathy , the courageous practice of radical forgiveness , and the difficult , yet essential , discipline of approaching others -- and ourselves -- with profound humility and searching self-awareness . This system assigns electoral votes to the 50 states and the District of Columbia based on population . When voters cast their ballots , they are actually selecting a slate of electors for the president . Most states use a winner-takes-all approach , where the candidate winning the popular vote in that state receives all its electoral votes , except for Maine and Nebraska , which distribute theirs proportionally . <p> A candidate must secure a minimum of 270 electoral votes out of a total of 538 to win the presidency . If the result is a 269-269 tie , the decision goes to the House of Representatives , where each state delegation casts one vote to break the deadlock . <p> Notably , it is possible for a candidate to win the presidency @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ W Bush in 2000 and Trump in 2016 . All IMF member countries are eligible to borrow from the IMF 's General Resources Account ( GRA ) at market-based interest rates , while only low-income countries are eligible to borrow at concessional rates ( currently at 0 per cent interest rates through June 2021 ) through the Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust ( PRGT ) . <h> What Are IMF 's Main Lending Instruments ? <p> * Stand-By Arrangement ( SBA ) : The SBA is intended for emerging and advanced market economies to address short-term or potential balance of payments problems . It typically covers a period of 12-24 months , but no @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ three-to-five years . <p> * Standby Credit Facility ( SCF ) : This instrument is used to address short-term or potential balance of payments problems , but intended for low-income countries under the PRGT . SCF has a repayment grace period of four years and a final maturity of eight years . <p> * Extended Fund Facility ( EFF ) : The EFF is designed for emerging and advanced market economies with longer-term balance of payments problems , where impediments to growth are considered structural . EFFs are typically approved for three years but may be extended . Repayments are due within four-to-ten years . <p> * Extended Credit Facility ( ECF ) : The ECF is the equivalent to the EFF for low-income countries and falls under the PRGT . It is designed to address medium-to-long-term structural issues . ECFs are also provided initially for three years but may be extended up to five years and include a five-year grace period , with a maturity of ten years . <p> * Rapid Financing Instrument ( RFI ) : The RFI provides rapid financial help to countries with urgent balance @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ range of urgent needs , like natural disasters , conflicts and commodity price shocks , and should be repaid within three and a quarter to five years . <p> * Rapid Credit Facility ( RCF ) : The RCF is also designed for rapid financial assistance during crises , but for low-income countries , and carries a grace period of five years and final maturity of 10 years . Unlike other facilities , RCFs and RFIs are provided in one outright loan disbursement , meaning no conventional conditionality needs to be met during the programme prior to disbursements . In response to Covid-19 , the IMF doubled how much countries can borrow under the RCF and RFI . <p> * Flexible Credit Line ( FCL ) : The FCL is designed for countries that the IMF deems to have strong policy frameworks and track records in economic performance that are in an immediate cash crunch -- but want to avoid the stigma and adverse market reaction . The FCL therefore does not involve ongoing conditions . Five countries have used the FCL so far ( Chile , Colombia , Mexico @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a three-to-five-year period . <p> * Precautionary and Liquidity Line ( PLL ) : The PLL is designed for the liquidity needs of countries with economic frameworks that the IMF deems sound , but with remaining problems that preclude them from using the FCL . Only the Republic of North Macedonia and Morocco have used the PLL so far . <p> * Catastrophe Containment and Relief Trust ( CCRT ) : It is different from the instruments above because it allows the IMF to provide grants , rather than loans , to the poorest countries in the form of debt relief . It was designed in 2015 during the Ebola outbreak to provide relief during catastrophic natural or public health disasters and free up resources to meet exceptional balance of payments needs . <p> * Policy Support Instrument ( PSI ) : The PSI was designed to give low-income countries a ' tool ' that enables them to secure IMF advice without financial assistance , with the intention of signalling confidence to donors , creditors and the general public that they are supported by the IMF . PSIs last between @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ conjunction with an ECF . <h> What Is India 's Stance At IMF Board ? <p> Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri said on Thursday the IMF 's board should look " deep within " and consider the facts before generously bailing out Pakistan . This can lock in weather patterns for several days or even a week . <p> Repeated blocking occurred this autumn . As winds move anticlockwise around high pressure systems in the Southern Hemisphere , blocking highs in the Tasman Sea can bring moist @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ coasts , increasing rainfall . But such high pressure systems also bring drier conditions for the interior of the southeast and much of Victoria and South Australia . <p> Often , these high pressure systems also bring northerly winds to Victoria , and this can cause warmer conditions across much of the state . <p> High pressure systems also tend to bring more clear and sunny conditions , which increases daytime temperatures in particular . Air in high pressure systems moves down towards the surface and this process causes warming , too . <p> Australia sits between the Pacific and Indian Oceans and is subject to their variability , so we often look there to help explain what 's happening with Australia 's climate . @@124508581 <p> In 1990 , India reported approximately 33 million cases of malaria . By 2019 , that number plummeted to 5.5 million due to a host of government interventions designed to reduce malaria incidence . Deaths from malaria saw a similar decline . New research finds that forests may have played a marginal role in avoiding additional malaria deaths , even though forests are generally considered malaria hotspots . <p> Forests -- with their dense canopies and humid weather -- are hotspots for malaria breeding and transmission in India . Malaria is transmitted when a female Anopheles mosquito carrying the Plasmodium parasite , bites a human host during feeding . Forested districts contributed to 32% of malaria cases and 42% of malaria mortality between 2000 and 2019 , while harbouring just 6.6% of the country 's population , government data shows . <p> " Mosquitos like the shade and humidity provided by forests . Forests provide ideal conditions for the entire duration of the mosquito 's 12-day life cycle . Forest cover also makes it harder to spot breeding habitats , which makes it difficult to clear them , " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- National Institute of Malaria Research . <p> But forest loss may also aggravate malaria transmission and mortality . The extent to which deforestation impacts malaria incidence and mortality in India is still being understood . Researchers from Ohio State University examined the impacts of deforestation on malaria mortality in 628 districts in rural areas , and found that on average , the loss of one square kilometre of forest resulted in 0.16 additional deaths due to Plasmodium falciparum per 100,000 people . P. falciparum causes the most number of malaria deaths in India . <p> The humidity and thick canopy of forests make them hotspots for malaria breeding and transmission . In India , forested districts contributed to 32% of malaria cases and 42% of malaria mortality between 2000 and 2019 . Image by Alosh Bennett via Wikimedia Commons ( CC BY 2.0 ) . <h> The vexed relationship between forests and malaria <p> Deforestation has been linked to a rise in malaria transmission in the Amazon in South America . A study analysing trends in deforestation and malaria in the Brazilian Amazon across 13 years found that on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ deforestation led to a 3.3% increase in malaria incidence . " The effect is larger in the interior and absent in outer Amazonian states where little forest remains , " a 2019 study , by Stanford researchers , says . <p> In this study too , the main driver is P. falciparum . The researchers hypothesise malaria incidence worsens in the interiors of the forest ( where forest cover is high , compared to the outer states where forest cover is low ) because after deforestation gives way to settlements and agriculture , " malaria exposure leads to temporary immunity ( in these parts ) , and housing quality and healthcare access improve . " <p> The study goes on to state that these effects are strongest in the interior in the early stages of deforestation . " As forest edge habitat increases , promoting mosquito vector breeding habitat , survival , and human biting rate , but the effects attenuate as forest loss progresses , forest edge area declines , and human settlements become larger and further removed from forest , " the study says . <p> But because @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , the same trends are not seen everywhere . In economic terms , the ecosystem services provided by the forest in preventing these additional deaths was calculated to be between $1.26 and $85.9 per hectare , per year . India has fifty-eight species of anopheline mosquitoes , of which six are major carriers of malaria . Increasing humidity , rainfall and rising temperatures due to climate change are projected to intensify and lengthen the transmission period for malaria . <p> The role of deforestation is less certain . @@124524073 <p> For successful transformation , innovation , collaboration , and continued investment are essential for long-term sustainability and growth . <p> The fashion , textile , and apparel industries have long been criticised for their significant contribution to pollution and resource depletion . Apparel production and logistics generate substantial waste and greenhouse gases , while frequently relying on cheap labour in developing countries . These industries are heavily resource-intensive , consuming large amounts of electricity , water , and chemicals , thereby exacerbating environmental degradation . Growing awareness among companies , consumers , manufacturers , and suppliers of these impacts on climate change and human lives is driving a shift in industry practices . <p> According to research by Hopkins et al . ( 2023 ) , the textile manufacturing sector consumes approximately 79 trillion litres of water annually , contributing around 20 per cent of global industrial water pollution . Millions of litres of untreated wastewater from dyeing and printing units are discharged into sewage systems , with colouring agents that are toxic and not readily biodegradable . The sector also accounts for about 35 per cent of ocean @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ industrial air pollution . Over time , the industry has impacted all life forms through soil , air , and water pollution , biodiversity loss , landfill growth , and ocean waste accumulation . <p> To address these issues , fashion , textile , and apparel companies must enact comprehensive , lasting change . Research indicates that the adoption of decarbonisation technologies , circular economy principles , and scientific innovations can significantly alter the sector 's impact . Companies are increasingly working to reduce carbon emissions across their supply chains ( Brydges , 2021 ) . Many are shifting from linear to circular business models , creating longer-lasting products ( Kazancoglu et al. , 2020 ) , with companies such as Patagonia leading the way . <p> Another study highlights that small and medium-sized fashion and apparel companies comprise 90 per cent of the sector globally . Yet , due to limitations in knowledge , technology , and finance , they contribute approximately 70 per cent of industry pollution ( Bartl &amp; Ipsmiller , 2023 ) . These businesses require practical , accessible solutions to minimise their environmental impact . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are propelled by a range of internal and external drivers towards adopting circular practices . Textile organisations in the UK clothing sector , for instance , face mounting pressure from governments and NGOs to integrate circular design practices that account for environmental and social impacts . National and international regulations are becoming significant motivating factors . <p> The rise of social media and the rapid dissemination of information have made consumers increasingly aware of fast fashion 's environmental and human costs . Particularly , younger consumers are demanding higher ethical standards and transparency from brands ( Karaosman and Marshall , 2023 ) . <p> Technical challenges , such as recycling fabrics , persist . Recycling is water-intensive and often results in inferior material quality when using more than 40 per cent recycled cotton . Separating blended fibres like cotton-polyester remains complex and costly . Brokered in 1960 by the World Bank , the IWT has long been hailed as a model of cross-border cooperation -- one that China has not emulated . ( Though its 1951 annexation of the water-rich Tibetan Plateau gave it control over the headwaters of Asia 's major rivers , China has refused to enter into a water-sharing treaty with any of its 18 downstream neighbours . ) <p> But treaties are built on mutual trust and good faith -- or , as the IWT 's preamble puts it , " a spirit of goodwill and friendship . " And while India has steadfastly adhered to the treaty for 65 years -- even when it meant compromising development in its water-stressed regions -- Pakistan has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ For example , it has used the treaty 's dispute-resolution mechanisms to drag India repeatedly into international arbitration over minor engineering differences and obstruct India 's ability to use its rightful share of water . Last year , when India formally sought to update the IWT -- to account for unanticipated factors like climate change , groundwater depletion , and population growth -- Pakistan refused to negotiate . <p> Meanwhile , Pakistan has waged what is effectively a proxy war by terrorism against India . The 2008 Mumbai massacre , in particular , is still etched in India 's national memory . In fact , the latest killings occurred shortly after the US extradited a key Mumbai plotter to India . Pakistan 's army chief , General Asim Munir , recently fanned the flames of conflict by urging Pakistanis to teach their children that Muslims are " different from Hindus in every possible way . " <p> International law is clear : when a treaty 's fundamental conditions collapse , or one party persistently violates them , the other party has the right to suspend or withdraw from the agreement @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ up the IWT , instead placing the treaty " in abeyance , " a term undefined in international law . Modi has thus retained strategic ambiguity , while sending a resolute message : resource-sharing comes with conditions . This is a warning , not a rupture . <p> To be sure , Pakistan claims that suspending the IWT amounts to an " act of war , " and has retaliated by suspending all bilateral agreements , including the 1972 Simla treaty , which governs peaceful dispute resolution . But this response not only ignores the reasons for India 's decision ; it also misrepresents the impact . <p> India is halting data sharing , design approvals , and inspections under the IWT , while opening the way for actions that Pakistani objections have obstructed , such as reservoir flushing and the desilting of riverbeds . But it is not disrupting current water flows . In fact , India does not have the infrastructure to divert the major rivers flowing to Pakistan , and its storage capacity on those rivers is negligible . <p> So , while India is imposing costs @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ accountable for state-sponsored terrorism , it is not punishing the Pakistani people . <p> The six rivers of the Indus Basin have sustained local civilisations for millennia , and they can continue to do so . But no country can be expected to uphold a peacetime treaty while suffering the consequences of an undeclared war . If Pakistan does not want India to turn off its taps by building new hydrological infrastructure , it must demonstrate a verifiable commitment to peace , arrest terrorist leaders , shut down terrorist-training camps , and end its support for cross-border violence . <p> The writer is Professor Emeritus of Strategic Studies at Center for Policy Research , New Delhi , and Fellow at the Robert Bosch Academy in Berlin . In a matter of hours , they torched eight rice plantations and liberated 730 people , people whose Lowcountry Creole language and culture Tubman could not even understand . Black @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's Sea Island cotton plantations after the Battle of Port Royal in November 1861 enlisted in the Second South Carolina Volunteers and risked their lives in the effort . <p> Using previous unexamined documents , including Tubman 's US Civil War Pension File , bills of sale , wills , marriage settlements , and estate papers from planters ; families , Fields-Black brings to life intergenerational , extended enslaved families , neighbors , praise-house members , and sweethearts forced to work in South Carolina 's deadly tidal rice swamps , sold , and separated during the antebellum period . From this urban past , egalitarian government structures , diplomacy , and complex economies spread across North America . So , when Europeans showed up in the 16th century , they encountered societies they did not understand -- those having developed differently from their own -- and whose power they often underestimated . <p> For centuries afterwards , Indigenous people maintained an upper hand and used Europeans in pursuit of their own interests . In Native Nations , we see how Mohawks closely controlled trade with the Dutch -- and influenced global markets -- and how Quapaws manipulated French colonists . Power dynamics shifted after the American Revolution , but Indigenous people continued to command much of the continent 's land and resources . Shawnee brothers Tecumseh and Tenskwatawa forged new alliances and encouraged a controversial new definition of Native identity to attempt to wall off American ambitions . The Cherokees created institutions to assert their sovereignty on the global stage , and the Kiowas used their @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ settlers across their territory . <p> In this important addition to the growing tradition of North American history centred on Indigenous nations , Kathleen DuVal shows how the definitions of power and means of exerting it shifted over time , but the sovereignty and influence of Native peoples remained a constant -- and will continue far into the future . <h> BiographyEvery Living Thing : The Great and Deadly Race to Know All Life , by Jason Roberts <p> In the 18th century , two men dedicated their lives to the same daunting task : identifying and describing all life on Earth . Their approaches could not have been more different . Carl Linnaeus , a pious Swedish doctor with a huckster 's flair , believed that life belonged in tidy , static categories . Georges-Louis de Buffon , an aristocratic polymath and keeper of France 's royal garden , viewed life as a dynamic , ever-changing swirl of complexities . Both began believing their work to be difficult , but not impossible -- how could the planet possibly hold more than a few thousand species ? Stunned by life @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . But in the process , they articulated starkly divergent views on nature , on humanity 's role in shaping the fate of our planet , and on humanity itself . <p> The rivalry between these two unique , driven individuals created reverberations that still echo today . Linnaeus , with the help of acolyte explorers he called " apostles " ( only half of whom returned alive ) , gave the world such concepts as mammal , primate and homo sapiens -- but he also denied species change and promulgated racist pseudo-science . Buffon coined the term reproduction , formulated early prototypes of evolution and genetics , and argued passionately against prejudice . It was a clash that , during their lifetimes , Buffon seemed to be winning . But their posthumous fates would take a very different turn . <h> Memoir or AutobiographyFeeding Ghosts : A Graphic Memoir , by Tessa Hulls <p> Tessa Hulls traces the reverberations of Chinese history across three generations of women in her family . @@124546916 <h> Impoundment of the Chenab River 's waters <p> Manu Kotwal The impoundment of the Chenab River 's waters represents a substantial modification to the established hydrological regime of the Indus River Basin . The Indus Waters Treaty ( IWT ) of 1960 , a cornerstone of transboundary water management between India and Pakistan , delineates specific water usage rights for both nations concerning the western rivers ( Indus , Jhelum , and Chenab ) . India 's allocation under the IWT primarily encompasses run-of-river projects and limited storage capabilities . Consequently , any large-scale obstruction , diversion , or impoundment that significantly diminishes the Chenab 's flow into Pakistan raises serious concerns regarding potential treaty violations and the ensuing implications for international arbitration . The historical context surrounding the Baghliar Dam project , often cited in discussions regarding Chenab River impoundment , underscores the complexities inherent in transboundary water resource management . While the dam 's construction was ostensibly motivated by power generation needs , the backdrop of regional tensions and security concerns , including alleged militant attacks , adds another layer to the analysis . Assertions that the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ exert pressure on Pakistan necessitate careful examination within the framework of international law and treaty obligations . Impact of Chenab River Impoundment on Pakistan 's Economy and Social Structure The Chenab River serves as a vital lifeline for Pakistan 's agricultural sector , contributing significantly to food security and economic stability . A reduction in Chenab 's water flow due to impoundment can trigger a cascade of adverse consequences : Agricultural Productivity Decline : The fertile plains of Punjab , heavily reliant on Chenab 's irrigation waters , would face diminished crop yields . This could lead to decreased agricultural output , impacting key crops like wheat , rice , and cotton , which are crucial for both domestic consumption and export earnings . Water Scarcity and Food Insecurity : Reduced water availability would exacerbate existing water scarcity issues , particularly in arid and semi-arid regions dependent on the Chenab . This could threaten food security , leading to price increases for essential commodities and potential social unrest . Economic Losses : The agricultural sector 's contribution to Pakistan 's GDP would decline , impacting livelihoods of farmers , agricultural @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ negatively affect the country 's trade balance . Displacement and Migration : Water scarcity and reduced agricultural productivity could trigger displacement of rural populations , leading to migration towards urban centers , placing strain on already overburdened urban infrastructure and resources . Social Disruption : Competition for scarce water resources could exacerbate social tensions and conflicts between different communities and regions , potentially leading to instability . Impact on Hydropower Generation : Pakistan also utilizes Chenab River water for hydropower generation . Reduced flows would compromise the capacity of existing hydropower plants , leading to energy shortages and increased reliance on alternative , potentially more expensive , energy sources . Rationale Behind the Indus Waters Treaty The Indus Waters Treaty was born out of the necessity to peacefully manage the shared water resources of the Indus River Basin following the partition of India and Pakistan in 1947 . The treaty allocated the three eastern rivers ( Sutlej , Beas , and Ravi ) primarily to India and the three western rivers ( Indus , Jhelum , and Chenab ) primarily to Pakistan , while also allowing India to use the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , subject to certain restrictions and design criteria . The treaty 's objectives were multifaceted : Prevent Water Conflicts : To avert potential conflicts arising from disputes over water sharing , which were particularly acute in the aftermath of partition . Ensure Equitable Water Distribution : To provide a framework for the equitable distribution of water resources between the two nations , safeguarding the water needs of both countries . Promote Cooperation : To foster cooperation and communication between India and Pakistan in the management of the Indus River Basin . Provide a Dispute Resolution Mechanism : To establish a mechanism for resolving disputes related to water sharing through a Permanent Indus Commission , neutral experts , or international arbitration . If India were to unilaterally disregard the terms and conditions of the IWT , the repercussions could be far-reaching : Breach of International Law : Violation of a legally binding international treaty would undermine India 's credibility and standing in the international community . Strained Bilateral Relations : Non-compliance would severely damage relations between India and Pakistan , exacerbating existing tensions and mistrust . International Condemnation : India could @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ about the stability of the region and the integrity of international agreements . Suspension of Cooperation : Pakistan might suspend cooperation on other issues of mutual interest , further isolating India in the region . Increased Risk of Conflict : Unilateral actions regarding water resources could escalate tensions and increase the risk of armed conflict between the two nations , particularly in a region already fraught with geopolitical instability . Economic Sanctions : In extreme cases , the international community could impose economic sanctions on India to compel compliance with the IWT . Legal Challenges : Pakistan could pursue legal remedies through international courts or arbitration tribunals to seek redress for treaty violations . The impoundment of the Chenab River 's waters presents a complex challenge , demanding careful consideration of the IWT 's provisions , the hydrological realities of the Indus River Basin , and the potential socio-economic consequences for Pakistan . While India has the right to utilize the western rivers for specific purposes within the treaty 's framework , any actions that substantially reduce the flow of the Chenab into Pakistan must be meticulously scrutinized to ensure @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ provisions could have devastating consequences for Pakistan 's agricultural sector , economy , and social stability , potentially leading to increased water scarcity , food insecurity , and social unrest . Furthermore , non-compliance with the IWT would undermine the treaty 's integrity , erode trust between India and Pakistan , and increase the risk of conflict in a volatile region.Therefore , it is imperative that both India and Pakistan adhere to the principles of good faith , transparency , and cooperation in the management of the Indus River Basin 's water resources . A commitment to dialogue , consultation , and the peaceful resolution of disputes is essential for ensuring the long-term stability and prosperity of the region . The potential for climate change to further exacerbate water scarcity in the region underscores the urgency of proactive and collaborative water management strategies . Increased variability in rainfall patterns , glacial melt , and rising temperatures will likely place even greater strain on the Indus River Basin 's water resources , making it imperative for India and Pakistan to work together to adapt to these challenges and ensure the equitable @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ may involve exploring innovative water conservation techniques , improving irrigation efficiency , and promoting water-wise agricultural practices . In conclusion , the Chenab River impoundment issue highlights the critical importance of adhering to the Indus Waters Treaty and promoting collaborative water management in the Indus River Basin . The potential consequences of non-compliance with the IWT are far-reaching , potentially jeopardizing the region 's stability and prosperity . By prioritizing dialogue , cooperation , and a commitment to the principles of international law , India and Pakistan can ensure the sustainable use of water resources and prevent water from becoming a source of conflict . The scientific community , civil society , and international organizations all have a role to play in supporting these efforts and promoting a more peaceful and sustainable future for the Indus River Basin . @@124560092 <p> Amillennia-old ecological marvel that has sustained Goa 's coastal communities since before recorded history is facing extinction . The khazan lands -- sophisticated networks of reclaimed wetlands and mangrove areas with ingenious water management systems -- are crumbling under the assault of modern threats while preservation efforts lag behind the pace of destruction . <p> Despite a flurry of government announcements and initiatives in recent months , the situation on the ground remains dire , with experts warning that more than 60% of these unique ecosystems are already in various stages of decay . <p> " Around 60% of the bundhs are in varying stages of breaking or collapse , " said khazan farmer Domingo Ferrao . " Many have already breached , others are crumbling , and some do n't have enough height to prevent water flowing over them into fields . They need immediate attention due to climate change considerations . " <p> What are khazans ? Understanding the living heritage <p> The khazans , which once covered approximately 17,500 hectares across eight of Goa 's eleven talukas , represent a remarkable feat of traditional ecological engineering @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , featuring intricate systems of bunds ( dykes ) , sluice gates called ' manos , ' water bodies known as ' poiems , ' and cultivable land . <p> It was titled ' A Study of Traditionally Managed Khazan Ecosystems of Ponda Taluka , Goa ' and was conducted by researchers Ranjita Sawaiker , Suraj Gaude , Samiksha Naik , Simran Chari , Tima Gaude , and Nischya Padwalkar . It documented the fragility and productivity of these systems and warned of threats from pollution , declining traditional skills , and youth disengagement . <p> The research highlights how these sophisticated systems have evolved over 2,000 years to create sustainable agricultural and aquaculture environments in saline conditions . <p> The sophisticated khazan system has deep historical roots , with archaeological evidence suggesting they date back to at least the 6th century . <p> At a recent workshop , Dr Pradip Sarmokadam , Member Secretary of the Goa State Biodiversity Board ( GSBB ) , emphasised their ecological significance : " Khazan land is not just one ecosystem . It 's where marshy land meets the estuarine ecosystem , creating @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reefs . " <p> This comprehensive range of activities has earned khazans the title of " food bowls of Goa , " underscoring their critical importance to local food security . <p> The khazans blend harmoniously with the local people , animals , plants , land , and water . The intricate system provides nesting , feeding , and breeding grounds to a wide variety of fauna , both resident and migratory . Beyond their agricultural value , they serve as natural defenses against sea-level rise , flooding , and other climate-related threats . <p> Traditional management systems and their decline <p> Originally maintained by Comunidades , these traditional institutions maintained the delicate balance required for khazan sustainability . The management changed following the Goa Agricultural Tenancy Act of 1964 , shifting responsibility to tenant associations supervised by government officials . <p> Some experts felt that in certain areas , fishing is seen as the more lucrative option and that this shift toward commercial fishing over traditional agriculture has undermined the integrated approach that made khazans sustainable . It was also pointed out that this is not the case everywhere @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ still work well together . However , the damage to khazan fields due to damaged bundhs has been a big concern in many villages , like in Neura , Tiswadi , where there have been multiple inspections to assess the damage . <p> At the Miramar Dialogues organised by WWF-India 's Goa State Office in January 2025 , former chief engineer of the Water Resources Department ( WRD ) and author of ' Khazans of Goa ' , Sandeep Nadkarni , elaborated that the former Chief Minister ( late ) Manohar Parrikar had considered establishing a cooperative system , but this initiative did n't materialise . <p> Loss of traditional knowledge <p> Perhaps the most insidious threat comes from within -- the breakdown of traditional management systems and the loss of specialised knowledge . The Ponda Taluka study documents how elderly community members revealed a concerning trend : youth lack interest in managing these traditional ecosystems through rice cultivation , fishing , and horticulture . This generational disconnect threatens the transmission of crucial knowledge about khazan maintenance . <p> " In the past , farmers knew about *khavte* ( breaking @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ they were repaired in time . But now , that is not the case as there is no common ownership , " explained Nadkarni . <p> More troubling are documented cases of intentional damage to the system . In proceedings before the High Court of Bombay at Goa , even the State 's advocate general acknowledged incidents of deliberate destruction of bundhs and sluice gates , typically aimed at facilitating illegal fishing activities without proper auctions . <p> The court has been explicit about this problem , stating in one order : " It is not as if these breaches are caused due to natural disasters or due to wear and tear that was not preventable , " while directing tenant associations to maintain strict vigilance against such sabotage . <p> Traditional maintenance techniques have been abandoned as well . The ancient practice of using estuarine soil for bundh repairs has been replaced with lateritic red mud , which lacks durability and washes away quickly . During the Miramar Dialogues , architect and educator Tallulah D'Silva specifically highlighted this issue , noting how modern bunds constructed with lateritic soil give @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ balance . <p> At this same dialogue , Sangeeta Sonak , Director of the Centre for Environment and Natural Resource Management , highlighted another critical issue : the lack of comprehensive data about khazan land in Goa . She noted that the often-cited figure of 18,951 hectares dates back to JC Almeida 's book published in 1967 , with no recent comprehensive assessment conducted . This data deficiency extends to other ecological aspects of Goa , including its rivers and water bodies . Without accurate , current data , effective conservation planning remains challenging . <p> Research and revival efforts <p> ICAR 's involvement extends beyond just studying the problem . In April 2025 , ICAR-Goa convened a significant meeting at its Merces experimental farm , bringing together farmers , scientists , and policymakers for a focused dialogue on the future of khazan lands . <p> The meeting was conducted under two NABARD-funded projects : ' Land Shaping Methods and Integrated Farming Systems Approach for Improving Livelihood Security of Farmers under Khazan Lands of Goa ' , and ' Evaluating the Performance of Multispecies Finfish Culture in Small Low-Cost Ponds @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Saline Region of Goa ' . <p> These projects are being implemented by ICAR-Goa in collaboration with the Goa Chamber of Commerce and Industry ( GCCI ) and the State Directorate of Agriculture . <p> Some other positive developments have emerged from research institutions . The Goa College of Agriculture and ICAR-Goa have been studying traditionally cultivated salt-tolerant rice varieties native to khazan lands , including Korgut and Assgo . Research published by the Department of Botany at Goa University documents these varieties ' unique morphological characteristics and promising grain quality .

@@124576776 <h> A decade-long search for a battery that can end the gasoline era <h> Can a small Massachusetts start-up perfect a battery that would make electric vehicles cheaper and more convenient than conventional cars ? <p> Can a small Massachusetts startup perfect a battery that would make electric vehicles cheaper and more convenient than conventional cars ? ( Felix Schmitt/The New York Times ) <p> Written by Jack Ewing <p> On a frigid day in early January , as she worked in her office in the Boston suburb of Billerica , Massachusetts , Siyu Huang received a two-word text message . <p> " Spinning wheels , " it said . Attached was a short video clip showing a car on rollers in an indoor testing center . <p> Story continues below this ad <p> There was nothing remarkable in the video . But to Huang , the CEO of Factorial Energy , the video was a milestone in a quest that had occupied a decade of her life . <p> Huang , her husband , Alex Yu , and their employees at Factorial had been working on a new kind @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that could turn the auto industry on its head -- if a daunting number of technical challenges could be overcome . <p> For Huang and her company , the battery had the potential to change the way consumers think about electric vehicles , give the United States and Europe a leg up on China , and help save the planet . <p> Factorial is one of dozens of companies trying to invent batteries that can charge faster , go farther , and make electric cars cheaper and more convenient than gasoline vehicles . Electric vehicles could be a potent weapon against climate change and urban air pollution . <p> Story continues below this ad <p> The video that landed in Huang 's phone was from Uwe Keller , the head of battery development at Mercedes-Benz , which had been supporting Factorial 's research with money and expertise . <p> The short clip , of a Mercedes sedan at a research lab near Stuttgart , Germany , signaled that the company had installed Factorial 's battery in a car -- and that it could actually make the wheels move . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that had begun while Huang and Yu were still graduate students at Cornell University . Until then , all their work had been in laboratories . Huang was excited that their invention was venturing into the world . <p> But there was still a long way to go . The Mercedes with a Factorial battery had n't yet been taken out on the road . <p> Story continues below this ad <p> Many startups have produced solid-state battery prototypes . Mercedes was looking for a bigger technological leap and encouraged Factorial to pursue solid state . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ name because it eliminates the liquid chemical mixture , known as an electrolyte , that helps transport energy-laden ions inside a battery . Liquid electrolytes are highly flammable . Replacing them with a solid or gelatinlike electrolyte makes batteries safer . <p> A battery that does n't overheat can be charged faster , perhaps in as little time as it takes to fill a car with gasoline . And solid-state batteries pack more energy into a smaller space . <p> But solid-state batteries have one big drawback : Such battery cells are more prone to grow spiky irregularities that cause short circuits . Vast riches await any company that can overcome this problem and develop a battery that is durable , safe and reasonably easy to manufacture at a reasonable price . <p> Factorial confronted that problem in 2022 , setting up a small pilot factory in Cheonan , South Korea , a city near Seoul known for its tech industry . The project became , in Huang 's words , " production hell . @@124577858 <h> The OECD 's review of AFOLU policies finds that ecosystem protection , technology standards , and R&amp;D investments offer the highest GHG mitigation per hectare , while subsidies and carbon taxes show moderate , context-dependent impacts . It calls for more robust evaluation and integration of climate goals across entire food systems . <p> The OECD report " Mitigating Climate Change in the Agriculture , Forestry and Other Land Use ( AFOLU ) Sectors : A Literature Review on Policy Effectiveness " , authored by Lauren Lee and Ada Ignaciuk , provides a sweeping analysis of policy measures aimed at tackling greenhouse gas ( GHG ) emissions in land-based sectors . Backed by contributions from the OECD 's Trade and Agriculture Directorate ( TAD ) , Environment Directorate ( ENV ) , and Economics Department ( ECO ) , the study draws from approximately 190 papers assessing the effectiveness of direct and indirect mitigation policies in OECD and G20 countries . Organized using the OECD 's Inclusive Forum on Climate Mitigation Approaches ( IFCMA ) typology , the report classifies policies into economic , regulatory , and other categories @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and potential to reduce emissions per unit of land . <h> Forest Protection Leads the Way in Climate Impact <p> Among all policy tools examined , those that prevent the destruction or degradation of natural carbon sinks , particularly zoning policies like protected areas , stood out as the most impactful . These policies , classified under framework regulations , were found to mitigate as much as 86 tonnes of CO2-equivalent per hectare per year , mainly by halting deforestation and conserving ecosystems such as tropical forests , peatlands , and mangroves . Their success lies in shielding carbon-rich landscapes from conversion to agricultural land . Yet , their effectiveness varies by location , governance quality , and enforcement capacity . Studies from Brazil , Indonesia , and Mexico confirmed strong results in emission reduction and cost-efficiency , particularly when targeted to areas of high deforestation risk and high carbon stock . <h> Technology and Innovation Offer High , Yet Unrealized , Potential <p> Another set of high-performing policies identified were technology standards , particularly those supporting advanced biofuels combined with carbon capture and storage . These policies promise up @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of these results stem from ex ante modeling , with limited real-world uptake due to high upfront costs and technical complexity . Similarly , government investment in research and development ( R&amp;D ) was shown to reduce emissions by 28 tonnes CO2-equivalent per hectare , largely by improving total factor productivity and advancing innovations in crop genetics , livestock breeding , and soil management . However , such policies often lack direct emissions data , making it harder to quantify benefits on a comparable scale . Nonetheless , the report underscores their critical role in the long-term transformation of agricultural systems and emissions trajectories . <h> Subsidies : Popular but Modest in Performance <p> Subsidies dominate the AFOLU policy landscape , both in frequency and political appeal , but their climate effectiveness is more modest , averaging just 5.3 tonnes CO2-equivalent per hectare . While subsidies aimed at afforestation , conservation tillage , and methane reduction in livestock can deliver positive outcomes , others , especially those tied to production incentives or land-use change , had mixed or uncertain effects . The risk of " subsidy lock-in , " where @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ as a major issue . Participation rates also matter : studies showed that higher payments can improve farmer uptake , but effectiveness declines if subsidies are not aligned with local ecological conditions . Furthermore , context-specific outcomes mean that what works in one country or landscape may underperform elsewhere . Policymakers are encouraged to stack or combine subsidies for multiple environmental benefits and use sunset clauses to limit long-term dependency . <h> Carbon Pricing : Theoretical Efficiency vs . Political Reality <p> Carbon taxes emerged in the review as theoretically powerful toolsfor emission reduction but remain rare in practice due to political resistance and measurement challenges in agriculture . The studies , largely ex ante simulations , suggested modest average reductions , around 6 tonnes CO2-equivalent per hectare , and highlighted carbon pricing 's ability to incentivize more efficient input use and discourage high-emission production . However , concerns over carbon leakage , where production shifts to jurisdictions with weaker policies , temper the benefits . When not applied uniformly across sectors and countries , such leakage can offset much of the emissions gains . Still , carbon taxes were @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ when revenues are recycled into support for affected farmers or innovation funds . <h> Mixed Returns from Trading Schemes and Voluntary Agreements <p> The report offers a cautiously critical view of carbon trading systems and voluntary offset marketsin the AFOLU sectors . While programs in California and Australia have issued millions of tonnes in credits , questions remain around the additionality , permanence , and verification of claimed reductions . Nearly 40% of trading system assessmentsreturned mixed or inconclusive results . Voluntary agreements , including private carbon markets and covenants between governments and producers , were found to have limited mitigation impact unless tied to strict monitoring and enforcement . Still , they may play a supporting role by increasing political acceptability or engaging stakeholders otherwise left out of regulatory approaches . <p> The OECD emphasizes that no single policy is a silver bullet . Effective mitigation requires a well-balanced mix of targeted interventions , grounded in local realities and supported by data . @@124596779 <h> Humans are killing helpful insects in hundreds of ways <p> Insects are all around us -- an ant on the sidewalk , a bee buzzing by , a butterfly floating on the breeze -- and they shape the world we experience . They pollinate flowering plants , decompose waste , control pests , and are critical links in food chains . Despite how much humans rely on insects , our actions are reducing their populations in many parts of the world . A recent study found that the United States lost more than 20% of its butterflies over the past two decades . Sadly , this rate of decline is not unusual . Many studies have found that insect populations are declining at 1% to 2% per year . To understand why this is happening , Status of Insects , an international research group we are part of , reviewed 175 recent studies on the causes of insect decline . We found hundreds of potential causes that are all highly connected , almost all of which stem directly or indirectly from human activities . The drivers of insect decline @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a few major sources : intensive agriculture , climate change , pollution , invasive species and habitat loss . Some drivers are bigger threats than others , but all of them play a role in causing insect declines . Importantly , many insects experience more than one of these stressors at the same time . Urban risks Picture a moth in a city park . It is threatened by habitat loss as the city grows , but its habitat may also be threatened by invasive plants that escape from gardens . At the same time , it is suffering from the effects of pollution -- light , air and noise pollution are common in urban areas . Light pollution is especially important for moths because they are attracted to artificial lights at night , and so are their predators . Spiders , for example , have learned to hunt in lit areas . When moth species that fly at night spend a lot of time around lights , they can expend a lot of energy , leaving less for other activities , such as pollinating plants . In addition to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ leaves during their caterpillar stage . And they provide food for many species of birds and bats , which play their own important roles in ecosystems . Risks on farmland and orchards Intensive agriculture is one of the most commonly discussed drivers of insect decline . It is also heavily connected to other causes . Consider native bees in agricultural areas . As agriculture expands , their native habitat is reduced . Agricultural landscapes also tend to have high levels of chemical pollution -- especially insecticides , fungicides , herbicides and fertilisers . Insecticides are designed to disrupt insect physiology and can directly harm bees , while herbicides indirectly disrupt bees by removing plants that provide food . Often , US farms also use honeybees , native to Europe , for pollination . These introduced bees are easier to manage but can spread diseases and parasites into native bee populations . Polluted water can also harm insects Humans often focus on insects such as bees and butterflies because they are more visible , but many insects spend much of their life underwater , where they face another set of threats @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ juveniles . The threats at this stage of life are no less severe but are entirely different from those facing adults . When water levels in streams or ponds decrease , that reduces young dragonflies ' habitat . These insects can also be threatened by water pollution from runoff and increases in water temperature with climate change .
